entries.title: Epoch
entries.text: One full pass of the training algorithm over the entire training dataset.

entries.title: Batch
entries.text: A subset of samples processed together before one optimizer step.

entries.title: Mini-batch
entries.text: A small batch used to trade off gradient quality and computation speed.

entries.title: Gradient Descent
entries.text: Optimization method that updates parameters in the direction of negative gradient.

entries.title: Backpropagation
entries.text: Algorithm for computing gradients through layered computational graphs.

entries.title: Overfitting
entries.text: When a model memorizes training data and fails to generalize to new data.

entries.title: Underfitting
entries.text: When a model is too simple to capture meaningful structure in data.

entries.title: Regularization
entries.text: Techniques that constrain model complexity to improve generalization.

entries.title: Dropout
entries.text: Training technique that randomly drops units to reduce co-adaptation.

entries.title: Learning Rate
entries.text: Step size controlling how much parameters change at each update.

entries.title: Loss Function
entries.text: Objective that quantifies prediction error and drives optimization.

entries.title: Activation Function
entries.text: Non-linear function applied to neural network layer outputs.

entries.title: Embedding
entries.text: Dense vector representation of discrete entities like words or IDs.

entries.title: Tokenization
entries.text: Process of splitting raw text into tokens for model input.

entries.title: Attention
entries.text: Mechanism that weights context elements by relevance to each query.

entries.title: Fine-tuning
entries.text: Adapting a pretrained model on task-specific data.

entries.title: Prompt
entries.text: Instructional text provided to a model at inference time.

entries.title: Inference
entries.text: Using a trained model to produce predictions on new data.

entries.title: Latency
entries.text: Time required to return a prediction after receiving input.

entries.title: Throughput
entries.text: Number of predictions processed per time unit.

entries.title: FLOPs
entries.text: Floating-point operations used as a rough compute-effort proxy.

entries.title: Batch Normalization
entries.text: Layer normalization of activations within mini-batches.

entries.title: Cross-validation
entries.text: Resampling strategy for estimating model performance robustness.

entries.title: Train/Validation/Test Split
entries.text: Partitioning data to train, tune, and evaluate models without leakage.

entries.title: Bias
entries.text: Systematic error component due to restrictive assumptions.

entries.title: Variance
entries.text: Sensitivity of model predictions to data fluctuations.

entries.title: Precision
entries.text: Fraction of predicted positives that are truly positive.

entries.title: Recall
entries.text: Fraction of actual positives that are correctly identified.

entries.title: F1 Score
entries.text: Harmonic mean of precision and recall for imbalanced tasks.

entries.title: ROC-AUC
entries.text: Area under ROC curve measuring ranking quality across thresholds.

entries.title: Confusion Matrix
entries.text: Table of true/false positives/negatives by class.

entries.title: Feature Engineering
entries.text: Transforming raw data into predictive inputs for models.

entries.title: Normalization
entries.text: Rescaling features to comparable ranges for stable optimization.

entries.title: Standardization
entries.text: Centering and scaling features to zero mean and unit variance.

entries.title: Outlier
entries.text: Observation that strongly deviates from typical data distribution.

entries.title: Data Drift
entries.text: Shift in production input distribution relative to training data.

entries.title: Model Drift
entries.text: Degradation in prediction quality over time due to environment change.

entries.title: Retraining
entries.text: Updating model parameters with fresher or broader data.

entries.title: Concept Drift
entries.text: Change in relationship between inputs and target labels.

entries.title: Baseline Model
entries.text: Simple benchmark used to contextualize advanced model gains.

entries.title: Hyperparameter
entries.text: External configuration controlling model structure or training behavior.

entries.title: Grid Search
entries.text: Exhaustive evaluation over predefined hyperparameter combinations.

entries.title: Random Search
entries.text: Sampling-based hyperparameter exploration over search space.

entries.title: Bayesian Optimization
entries.text: Sequential model-based search balancing exploration and exploitation.

entries.title: Early Stopping
entries.text: Stopping training when validation performance stops improving.

entries.title: Ensemble
entries.text: Combining multiple models to improve accuracy or robustness.

entries.title: Bagging
entries.text: Ensemble method training independent learners on bootstrapped samples.

entries.title: Boosting
entries.text: Sequential ensemble approach emphasizing previously mispredicted examples.

entries.title: Kernel Trick
entries.text: Implicit mapping enabling linear separators in transformed space.

entries.title: Margin
entries.text: Distance between decision boundary and nearest training points.

entries.title: Centroid
entries.text: Mean vector representing a cluster center in k-means.

entries.title: Explained Variance
entries.text: Fraction of total variance captured by selected components.

entries.title: Policy
entries.text: Mapping from states to actions in reinforcement learning.

entries.title: Value Function
entries.text: Expected long-term return from a state or state-action pair.

entries.title: Reward
entries.text: Scalar feedback signal defining task objective in RL.

entries.title: Exploration
entries.text: Trying uncertain actions to discover better future returns.

entries.title: Exploitation
entries.text: Choosing currently best-known action to maximize immediate return.

entries.title: Replay Buffer
entries.text: Memory store of transitions sampled during DQN training.

entries.title: Target Network
entries.text: Delayed copy of Q-network used to stabilize temporal-difference targets.

entries.title: Policy Gradient
entries.text: Family of methods optimizing policy directly via gradient ascent.

entries.title: KL Divergence
entries.text: Measure of difference between probability distributions.

entries.title: Latent Space
entries.text: Compressed representation space learned by generative models.

entries.title: Mode Collapse
entries.text: GAN failure mode where generator outputs limited variety.

entries.title: Pruning
entries.text: Removing less important parameters to reduce model size and cost.

entries.title: Quantization-aware Training
entries.text: Training with quantization effects simulated to preserve accuracy.

entries.title: Distillation Temperature
entries.text: Softmax temperature controlling teacher-soft-target smoothness.

entries.title: Top-k Accuracy
entries.text: Metric counting prediction as correct if true label is in top-k outputs.

entries.title: What's the difference between AI, ML, and deep learning?
entries.text: AI is the broad field, ML is a subset using data-driven learning, and deep learning is ML based on multi-layer neural networks.

entries.title: When should I use a Random Forest vs a neural network?
entries.text: Use Random Forest as a strong tabular baseline with limited data and interpretability needs; prefer neural nets for large-scale unstructured data and representation learning.

entries.title: Why does my model perform great in training but poorly in production?
entries.text: Common causes include overfitting, data leakage, data drift, and target definition mismatch between offline and online environments.

entries.title: Do I need a GPU to train models?
entries.text: Not always. Classical ML usually runs on CPU, while deep learning training is typically much faster on GPUs.

entries.title: How do I know if I have enough data?
entries.text: Track validation learning curves and performance variance. If metrics plateau early and error remains high, you may need better data or features.

entries.title: What's the cheapest way to fine-tune an LLM?
entries.text: Start with prompt optimization and retrieval grounding, then use parameter-efficient methods before full fine-tuning.

entries.title: What is the first model I should try for tabular classification?
entries.text: Try logistic regression and random forest baselines first to establish reference performance and feature quality.

entries.title: How do I choose an evaluation metric?
entries.text: Choose metrics tied to decision costs. For imbalance, prioritize precision/recall/F1 over raw accuracy.

entries.title: What causes unstable training loss?
entries.text: Learning rate may be too high, gradients may explode, or data preprocessing may be inconsistent.

entries.title: Should I normalize inputs for tree models?
entries.text: Usually unnecessary for trees, but still useful when combining with linear or neural models in the same pipeline.

entries.title: When is PCA useful?
entries.text: PCA helps when features are highly correlated and you need dimensionality reduction for speed, denoising, or visualization.

entries.title: How can I reduce inference latency?
entries.text: Use batching carefully, optimize serving hardware, and apply quantization or pruning if accuracy constraints allow.

entries.title: What is concept drift and how do I detect it?
entries.text: Concept drift is change in input-target relationship. Detect with monitoring on delayed labels and rolling performance slices.

entries.title: Is cross-validation always required?
entries.text: Not always, but it is strongly recommended on smaller datasets to reduce variance in model selection decisions.

entries.title: How often should I retrain?
entries.text: Use trigger-based policies from drift and KPI degradation rather than fixed calendars when possible.

entries.title: What is a good baseline for computer vision?
entries.text: Transfer learning with a pretrained CNN is often the fastest and strongest baseline for image tasks.

entries.title: When should I use transformers over LSTMs?
entries.text: Transformers dominate for long-range dependencies and parallel training; LSTMs can still be practical for compact sequence workloads.

entries.title: How do I prevent overfitting in deep networks?
entries.text: Use regularization, dropout, early stopping, augmentation, and stronger validation discipline.

entries.title: What is the difference between pruning and quantization?
entries.text: Pruning removes parameters or channels; quantization reduces numeric precision. They are often complementary.

entries.title: Can I deploy one model for all user segments?
entries.text: Sometimes, but segment-aware evaluation is required to avoid hidden performance disparities and fairness regressions.

entries.title: How do I choose k in k-means?
entries.text: Use domain constraints, elbow/silhouette diagnostics, and stability checks across random initializations.

entries.title: What are common GAN failure modes?
entries.text: Mode collapse, training instability, and discriminator overpowering are frequent in practice.

entries.title: Is Bayesian optimization always better than random search?
entries.text: Not always. On small budgets or noisy objectives, random search can be competitive and simpler to parallelize.

entries.title: How do I monitor a model without immediate labels?
entries.text: Track proxy metrics such as feature drift, prediction entropy, and business funnel indicators until labels arrive.

entries.title: What should go into an ML problem statement?
entries.text: Business objective, target definition, constraints, acceptable risk, decision threshold policy, and success KPI.
